steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: First Past the Post (FPTP): used for UK general elections. The country is divided into 650 constituencies; each elects one MP by simple plurality (most votes wins). Strengths: simple to understand, produces strong majority governments, clear MP-constituency link. Weaknesses: disproportional (winning party often gets a majority of seats with less than 50% of votes), wasted votes in safe seats, smaller parties under-represented.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Proportional representation (PR): party seats match their vote share. Used in many European countries. The Additional Member System (AMS) is used for Scottish Parliament and Welsh Senedd elections. The Single Transferable Vote (STV) is used in Northern Ireland. PR is fairer but often produces coalition governments.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The franchise (right to vote): expanded over centuries: 1832 (property-owning men), 1867 (urban working men), 1918 (all men over 21, women over 30), 1928 (equal suffrage at 21), 1969 (voting age reduced to 18), 2015 (16 for Scottish independence referendum). Debates: should the voting age be lowered to 16 for all UK elections?

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Types of elections: general elections (MPs, FPTP), devolved elections (MSPs/MSs/MLAs, AMS/STV), local elections (councillors, FPTP), European elections (closed list PR, now irrelevant post-Brexit), Police and Crime Commissioner elections (supplementary vote), and by-elections.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: FPTP = simple, strong government, UNFAIR. PR = fair, representative, potentially UNSTABLE. Franchise expanded: property men -> all men -> women -> age 18 -> age 16 (Scotland). Each step was contested. 2019 result shows FPTP distortion: 44% votes -> 56% seats. PR would be fairer but may reduce stability.
